request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 6 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 6 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

remedy_content.text:
# Verification Before Completion Claims

Before reporting any fix, change, or validation/lint/test check as complete or
passing, run its declared verification command and report the actual result
plainly. Never state that a check passed, a fix works, or a change is
verified without having executed the check first — this applies to releases,
ordinary bug fixes, lint/validation runs, and any other completion claim.

structured_output.routing_rationale: All six incidents are the same shape: the agent asserted a fix/change/check was done, working, or passing without ever executing the declared verification, lint, or test command. This is a one-line standing-rule problem, not a multi-step procedure — no branching logic or tool sequence is needed, just "run it before you claim it." A claude-md rule for exactly this pattern already exists (R2, "Fake Release Discipline"), but its text is scoped narrowly to "release" completions. The new incidents show the identical failure occurring for ordinary fixes and validation/lint checks outside any release context, so the correct move is to broaden R2's existing text rather than mint a new artifact. A hook is not viable: there is no mechanical signal to intercept a natural-language "it passed"/"it's fixed" claim before it's emitted. A skill is unwarranted per merge bias — R1 already exists as a skill for this same failure mode, so adding a second skill-shaped remedy would duplicate enforcement; since a cheaper claude-md path is available and already installed, we extend that one instead of touching R1. benchmark-only would discard a fix we already know is installable and applicable.
